articles.title: Russia 'tearing Kyiv apart', mayor says, as strikes paralyse traffic
articles.body:
Russian attacks on key infrastructure were "tearing Kyiv apart", the city's mayor said Friday, as strikes on a bridge linking the capital's east and west brought traffic to a standstill.
President Volodymyr Zelensky accused his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, of ripping up the rulebook of armed conflict by sanctioning massive attacks on civilian areas, an accusation the Kremlin has rejected.
The grinding conflict, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, has largely focused on ground fighting in the east, with Kyiv mostly spared from the devastation wrought near the frontline.
But Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city should now be on a war footing.
"The capital is in a very dramatic situation," he posted on Telegram. "It's no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we lived in peacetime."
"The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart."
His message came as the authorities shut one of Kyiv's main bridges and restricted movement on a second after another wave of deadly strikes by fast-moving, jet-powered drones.
Traffic heavily disturbed
Long lines of stationary cars and buses were gridlocked on main roads as commuters sought alternative routes — or even made their way on foot.
"I've been travelling for three hours... to get to work," said Tetiana Osypenko, a 49-year-old seamstress whose bus was stuck in a traffic jam.
"There's just no way to get there. Nothing. It's impossible to cross the bridges today," she said.
Traffic built up due to the complete closure to all vehicles going in both directions on the Southern Bridge, one of eight bridges connecting the east and west of Kyiv over the Dnipro river.
The cable-stayed bridge has been hit several times since Thursday, with new strikes confirmed by Klitschko on Friday afternoon.
The Paton Bridge, further north, was open in one direction only, though there were no reports that it had been struck.
On X, Zelensky accused Putin of last month declaring there were "no rules now", citing unnamed intelligence and people around Putin.
"The Russians couldn't occupy us. So now they are doing massive attacks and massive killings," Zelensky said in remarks first made in a Financial Times interview.
The Kremlin made no immediate public response to the claim.
Daily bombing fear
Kyiv has been increasingly under aerial bombardment in recent months, putting the city on near-constant alert and disrupting daily life.
Air raid sirens warning of approaching threats in the skies sound almost round the clock, urging the city's estimated three million people to seek shelter.
Repeated strikes on trains and petrol stations have already hit the rail and road networks while attacks on energy facilities threaten power and heating as winter approaches.
Osypenko, the seamstress, said previous disruptions to subway services during air raids have forced her to spend the night in a metro station near the Southern Bridge.
Loss of earnings compounds the financial pressures caused by the war, she added. "You just spend the whole day feeling completely beaten down."
The latest Russian attacks killed one person and wounded at least two other people when a 25-storey residential building was hit in southeast Kyiv.
Two people were killed and dozens more injured when Russian shelling hit residential areas in the eastern city of Kharkiv, city mayor Igor Terekhov said on Telegram.
'Political will'
Zelensky urged tougher sanctions to prevent Russia from manufacturing jet-powered drones, which are harder to intercept.
Russia's production of the weapons was "critically dependent" on foreign components, he wrote on social media on Friday.
"Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line. What is needed is the political will of these countries," he added.
Zelensky has repeatedly called on Ukraine's Western allies for more military support, particularly for US-made Patriot missile interceptors.
On Thursday, he said Ukraine had used its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, without disclosing where or what it had been used against.
He also said Ukraine was testing five of its own interceptors against drones.
Ukraine's military on Friday said it struck an oil refinery in Volgograd and another facility in Samara, both in southwest Russia, for allegedly supplying fuel to Russian forces.
Kyiv also dismissed reports that its F-16 fighter jets — another key tool used against jet-powered drones — could be grounded due to delays in maintenance inspections and the supply of parts.
But Zelensky told the Financial Times that around half of Ukraine's fleet was spending lengthy maintenance periods in Europe.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia launched more than 90 attacks in Yemen in 24 hours, Houthis claim - report
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia has carried out 94 airstrikes in Yemen over the past 24 hours, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarie claimed, according to a Friday Ynet report.
The attacks were allegedly carried out using fighter jets and missiles and targeted civilian sites in the provinces of Sana'a, Saada, Taiz, Hajjah, Amran, and Al Bayda.
Sarie alleged the strikes caused civilian deaths and injuries, according to the report.
He also claimed that the total number of Saudi strikes on Yemen since the beginning of the escalation has reached 1,350.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Friday that it had intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Reuters reported on Friday.
Tensions between Saudi Arabia, Houthis remain high
The Houthis threatened to target bridges in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for airstrikes the group claims were carried out by the Saudi military, a Sana'a military source told Lebanese outlet Al Akhbar on Monday.
According to the source, Saudi Arabian airstrikes have targeted Yemeni bridges and other civilian infrastructure while claiming they were missile launch platforms.
"Civilian bridges are not used for military purposes," the source said, calling the Saudi practice "utter bankruptcy."
Saudi Arabia prepares offensive against Houthis
Reuters also reported Friday that Saudi Arabia is preparing an offensive against the Houthis aimed at breaking the group's grip on the coast and securing Red Sea shipping routes.
According to six people familiar with the preparations, the operation is expected to begin in the coming weeks. It would be led on the ground by Yemeni forces overseen by Riyadh and supported by Saudi airstrikes.
The objective of the offensive is to reverse gains made by the Houthis last month, when they seized control of parts of the coast, particularly around the Bab al Mandab Strait, according to the report.
Saudi officials are considering two possible options for the assault, according to Gulf and Yemeni officials. One would involve a narrowly focused attack around Bab al Mandab, while the other would involve a broader offensive with synchronized attacks on multiple fronts across Yemen, including in Al Bayda, Marib, Taiz, and Al Jawf.
More than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilized in the offensive, depending on the scale, the officials all said.
Spokespeople for the Saudi and Yemeni governments, the Houthi group and the US military didn't immediately respond to requests for comment about the Saudi plans.
Bab al-Mandab is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that's assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed by the Iran conflict.
Tzvi Jasper contributed to this report.

articles.title: Pentagon planning for more naval forces in Mideast as Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran - report
articles.body:
The US military is planning a potential increase of thousands of naval forces in the Middle East in the coming weeks, the Washington Post reported on Friday.
The Pentagon intends to move up three aircraft carriers and escort ships into the region to create flexibility in overseeing the war, according to the report.
Administration deliberates next move on Iran
The planning comes as US President Donald Trump’s administration deliberates on how to approach the Iran war, which has now entered its eighth month, causing dissatisfaction among the American public and roiling the global economy, according to the WP.
Additional forces deployed to the region will include 20,000 troops, up to 150 fighter jets, and numerous destroyers to launch and fend off missile attacks, it added.
The USS George Washington, last deployed to the Arabian Sea, the USS George H.W. Bush, currently in the Indian Ocean, and the USS Theodore Roosevelt are among the carriers involved in the discussions, the WP said, citing an earlier report by the Wall Street Journal.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt was deployed recently to San Diego and must make its way across the Pacific Ocean, it added.
The plans come as Trump considers renewing strikes on Iran following November’s midterm elections, the WP said, citing US officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity. 
In an interview published by Time magazine on Thursday, the US President said that it’s  “possible” he will ramp up bombing after the midterms, according to the WP’s report. 
50,000 troops are currently deployed
Around 50,000 US troops are currently deployed in the Middle East, the WP cited US officials as saying.
The Navy, according to the report, recently deployed the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, a three-ship task force of Marines and sailors from California.
The Boxer Amphibious Ready Group, a similar unit, has already been in the Middle East for months and includes more than 4,000 sailors and Marines, the report added, citing officials.
If Trump decides against expanding the conflict with Iran, the recently deployed vessels would likely replace those that have been there for months, the WP cited officials as saying.
The war, according to the report, has challenged the Pentagon as troop morale declines and ships require additional maintenance.
The war with Iran has cost the US billions of dollars, it added, left more than 800 troops wounded, and killed at least 19 others.

articles.title: 41 Ukrainians Return From Russian Occupation via Volyn, Including 9 children
articles.body:
Forty-one Ukrainian citizens, including four children and five teenagers, successfully returned from Russian-occupied territories through the Mokrany-Domanove checkpoint in the Volyn region.
The returns, carried out through the crossing on Ukraine’s border with Belarus in August and September, were organized with the help of partner organizations and the office of Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, Dmytro Lubinets.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In a statement on Friday, Oct. 2, Lubinets described the experiences of several citizens who returned, while also pointing to civilians who remain trapped in occupied areas.
“For each of them, this is not just a border crossing. It marks the end of months or years of life under occupation – with fear, pressure, persecution and constant uncertainty,” Lubinets said.
He singled out the town of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, which he previously called a “death trap” and where Ukrainian authorities say a man-made humanitarian catastrophe is unfolding.
Detentions, mobilization threats and forced treatment
Volyn, bordering Poland and Belarus, remains one of few routes home for Ukrainians leaving Russian-occupied territories, as there is no safe way to cross the frontline directly. Those who seek to escape often have to leave through Russia and travel via third countries before re-entering Ukraine.
Among those who returned was a family that was able to leave after the father was released from captivity. According to Lubinets, their eldest son has also been held captive since April 17, 2022.
G7 Members Agree to Release Up to 100M Barrels of Oil Reserves to Curb Fuel Prices
The mother and her younger son had been under constant monitoring by occupational law enforcement and medical services.
According to the family, they were previously placed in a detention facility under the pretext of receiving medical care, where they were held against their will and subjected to forced treatment.
A young medic was also brought out of the occupied territories moments before she would have effectively been mobilized into Russia’s armed forces. “A little longer, and her life could have followed a path that was decided for her under occupation,” Lubinets wrote in the statement.
A man that has been detained several times in the occupied territories managed to return as well. According to Lubinets, he has been held in basements, with his Ukrainian passport confiscated.
“Occupation is not just territory on a map,” Lubinets said. “Its the loss of freedom, documents, housing, work, connection with loved ones and a sense of safety.”
Support continues after return
Under a joint project with the charitable foundation Caritas Ukraine, returnees receive help restoring documents, temporary housing, financial support, as well as psychological and social assistance, and tickets for onward travel.
The project assisted 1,140 Ukrainian nationals through August and September, including those evacuated with the help of the ombudsman’s office.
Kyiv Post could not independently verify these figures.
According to Lubinets, the office receives daily requests from people seeking to leave the occupied territories. His team reviews each case, subsequently searching for possible routes while working with international partners and third countries.
Oleshky remains cut off
The ombudsman warned that the situation remains particularly severe in Oleshky and nearby settlements, where elderly people, people with disabilities and families continue to live under constant danger.
The city is located in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region on the left bank of the Dnipro River, about 5 km (3 miles) southeast of the city of Kherson, and has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Residents have limited access to food, water, medicine, medical care and communications, and leaving safely remains extremely difficult, with people frequently walking through mined fields just to escape.
On July 16, Lubinets said Russian authorities had failed to uphold previously agreed arrangements for a humanitarian evacuation from the occupied town.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) was prepared to take part in the evacuation within its mandate, while Ukrainian security and defense forces made arrangements for a ceasefire during the proposed operation.
At the time, his office had received 176 appeals about the situation in Oleshky and verified at least 358 people in urgent need of help to leave.
Lubinets estimated that more than 6,000 people, including around 200 children, could still be in the town and surrounding area, though the figures could not be independently verified due to tight Russian restrictions on information.
“They see no other way to escape this hell,” he said, adding that “they risk stepping on mines or being hit by drones, yet they go because remaining in Oleshky is even worse for them.”
Ukrainian officials said on Monday, Sept. 28 that remaining residents have been forced to eat dogs and weeds as Russian forces prevent them from leaving and block supplies from entering the city. Ukrainian forces have resolved to use drones to drop food because ground convoys cannot safely enter the city, although the deliveries cannot replace regular humanitarian access.
On Wednesday, Sept. 30, Ukraine initiated an urgent meeting of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) over the worsening situation in the city.
Around the same time, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned that the Kremlin is preparing to stage dozens of videos featuring residents of occupied Oleshky, forcing them to claim they are “well-fed and happy.”
Meanwhile, the Kremlin continues denying that it targets civilians in its fifth year of war and has also sought to shift the blame for the crisis in Oleshky onto Kyiv.

articles.title: On the run for 20 years, Ugandan warlord Kony still 'active' within the Lord's Resistance Army
articles.body:
On the run for 20 years, Ugandan warlord Kony still 'active' within the Lord's Resistance Army
In recent months, the eastern Central African Republic has been hit by several attacks attributed to the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA), a Ugandan militia infamous for its massacres and mass abductions of children in the 1990s and 2000s. The group's leader, Joseph Kony, wanted by the International Criminal Court for more than 20 years, remains at large. FRANCE 24 spoke to Leonie von Braun, the ICC’s lead investigator on the Kony case, about the group's resurgence.
Joseph Kony, the fugitive rebel leader of the Lord's Resistance Army, has been wanted by the ICC for more than 20 years.
A former altar boy and self-proclaimed messiah, prophet and messenger of God, Kony founded the rebel group in 1987 with the aim of overthrowing Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni and establishing a theocratic regime based on the ten commandments in the Bible.
The LRA's bloody insurgency is one of Africa's longest and most brutal conflicts.
It has claimed more than 100,000 lives and displaced more than two million people, mainly in northern Uganda, according to the UN.
The group carried out numerous massacres and kidnappings of children, who were recruited by the thousands to fight or to satisfy Kony's commanders' sexual appetites.
Resurgence in the Central African Republic
Driven out of the country in 2006 by the national army, the group gradually faded from the public eye, although it remains active in isolated border areas of Central Africa.
But in recent months, the LRA has once again made headlines. Central African authorities are concerned about a resurgence of attacks in the east and southeast of the country. At least 25 children have been abducted there during several raids on villages in attacks attributed to Kony’s notorious militia.
FRANCE 24 spoke to Leonie von Braun, Senior Trial Lawyer at the ICC and lead investigator in the Joseph Kony case, about the group's resurgence.
The Lord’s Resistance Army seemed to have virtually disappeared in recent years. How do you interpret these new attacks?
Leonie von Braun: The LRA is much less powerful than it was in the 2000s. The organisation used to be highly hierarchical, with four brigades, each estimated to have several hundred fighters. Today, they operate on a much smaller scale.
However, they remain active, employing a survival strategy very similar to the one used in northern Uganda and, later, when they were driven out of their country, in South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
In the Central African Republic, we are seeing attacks on villages located in the region where they have set up their camps. Civilians are being abducted and enslaved.
This information shows that they are still armed and ready to commit acts of violence. The more people they abduct, the stronger they become. They have always acted this way. They kidnap children because they are easy to indoctrinate, and they turn them into fighters. Within a few years, they have soldiers capable of handling rifles and throwing grenades.
Even though the LRA has been weakened, the risk remains very high for local populations due to these kinds of organisations, which are willing to commit the worst atrocities to ensure their survival.
Read moreVideo: Ugandan city still scarred by Lord's Resistance Army atrocities
You mention the recruitment of children, yet this movement defines itself as Christian. Is this recruitment based on religious grounds?
The LRA has its origins in another Ugandan rebel movement, the “Holy Spirit Movement", founded in the 1980s by a woman named Alice Auma. She called herself Lakwena, after the “spirit” from whom she claimed to receive orders. This group had already attempted – and failed – to overthrow the government.
Joseph Kony subsequently took control of it. The LRA is not a Christian movement in the strict sense but a syncretic movement that blends Christianity with local beliefs. Its leader uses belief in spirits to instill fear among his troops. But indoctrination is carried out primarily through violence.
Children are subjected to initiation rites – extremely violent acts that literally break them – and then the rules are explained to them. For example, dropping a pot of food is punished with severe beatings, just as is refusing to have sex with a commander. An escape attempt is tantamount to death or a near-death experience. Children are subjected to a system of the most severe disciplinary measures, with numerous rules designed to extract total obedience from them.
Read moreFormer Ugandan child soldier-turned-rebel commander sentenced to 25 years at ICC
The ICC issued an arrest warrant for Joseph Kony in 2005. He has been the subject of an intense manhunt, including by the United States, which offered a $5 million reward for any information leading to his capture. How can we explain the fact that he is still on the run?
There have been massive media campaigns on social media calling for his arrest, particularly around 2012 and when the United States deployed US special forces to Central Africa to track him down.
His ability to stay under the radar can be attributed to several factors. On the one hand, his knowledge of the terrain and his in-depth understanding of the region’s geography; on the other hand, his ability to endure hardship.
This is not, of course, meant to praise him, but it must be acknowledged that Joseph Kony has demonstrated extreme physical and psychological resilience. He has taught the members of his group how to survive in the bush under extremely difficult conditions, how to anticipate changes in the area, and has managed to set up an intelligence network – technologically unsophisticated but highly effective – to evade surveillance and, above all, continue carrying out criminal operations.
Furthermore, the very nature of this group poses a major problem because it includes a large number of children. Any planning for an operation must take into account the risk faced by those who are unarmed, who are not combatants, and who are in no way responsible for their situation. It is therefore essential to find the right moment to act. The situation is made all the more complicated by the fact that it is difficult to obtain reliable and up-to-date information about this group.
Read moreOvercoming the trauma: Singing lessons help former child soldiers in Uganda
What do we know today about Joseph Kony? He is reportedly 65 years old. Are you certain he is still alive?
We are monitoring the Lord’s Resistance Army very closely and are doing everything in our power to secure the surrender and arrest of its leader. The latest information we have indicates that he is still alive. He is not the only leader within this group. There is a hierarchy. And given his age, we might infer that he is not on the front lines in terms of operations. But he is still active and very much present within the LRA.
After 20 years of investigation, do you think it is still possible that Joseph Kony will one day be brought to justice? What does this case mean for the ICC’s credibility?
This case is particularly significant because of the gravity of the crimes committed against the most vulnerable members of society. The evidence shows that thousands of children and women were abducted during the period falling within our jurisdiction alone – from July 1, 2002, to December 31, 2005. This is a case of considerable magnitude – the largest we have ever handled involving crimes against children.
In a sense, this case tests the limits of the ICC, as we do not have our own police force. We issue arrest warrants, the recognition and execution of which depend on the cooperation of States. But it is extremely important for us to finally bring him to justice, and we are convinced that this is still possible. No one could have imagined that Milosevic, Charles Taylor, and many others would be held accountable for their actions before international justice. We are therefore continuing our efforts.

articles.title: The American-Ukrainian investment fund has concluded its first deal in the field of "critical minerals" — media
articles.body:
The American-Ukrainian investment fund has concluded its first deal in the field of "critical minerals" — media
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukraine Reconstruction Fund has concluded its first deal with BGV Group and launched four more projects. The total value of the investments reached $70 million.
The joint U.S.-Ukrainian investment fund established to rebuild the country has concluded its first deal in the critical minerals sector and launched four other new projects. A senior U.S. official told Reuters, reports UNN.
Details
The fund, established under the minerals agreement (signed by both countries in April last year at the initiative of U.S. President Donald Trump), focuses on five strategic sectors, ranging from mineral extraction and defense to energy and infrastructure.
Conor Coleman, head of the investment division at the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), said that the total value of the fund’s projects currently stands at around $70 million, demonstrating Washington’s support for Kyiv in its prolonged war with Russia.
"It is extremely important for the Ukrainian people that we are investing right now," Coleman said in an interview, referring to the ongoing destruction Ukraine is suffering ahead of another winter.
The first, long-awaited minerals deal involves an investment of around $30 million in a "joint investment platform" with BGV Group, a company founded by Hennadiy Butkevych, a billionaire and co-owner of Ukraine’s largest supermarket chain, "ATB."
According to Coleman, at the initial stage, the activity will focus on early-stage mining projects across Ukraine, specifically deposits of rare-earth metals, uranium, beryllium, and zirconium.
"All of these resources are included on the U.S. list of critical minerals, so this aligns very well with the priorities of the American administration," Coleman said.
In addition
The two other new projects announced on Friday are aimed at strengthening Ukraine’s electricity and heating networks in response to the increasing frequency of Russian attacks on critical infrastructure ahead of winter.
Coleman said that one of these projects will complement a nearly $100 million loan that the DFC has just agreed to provide to Ukraine’s largest private energy company, DTEK. The funds will be used to create a new battery system capable of providing backup power to approximately 600,000 Ukrainian households for two hours.
The project also provides for "access to capital in the event of damage." The fund will also acquire a stake in a cogeneration platform (a system for the combined production of thermal and electrical energy) intended to create and operate a number of "energy hubs" whose purpose is to restore damaged electricity and heat supplies for households.
Coleman also noted that the fund is seeking additional capital to expand its capacity.

articles.title: Houthi projectile hits school in Saudi Arabia's Najran: Civil Defense
articles.body:
Mohammad Sio
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
A projectile launched by Yemen's Houthi group struck a school in Saudi Arabia's southern city of Najran on Friday, causing material damage, the Saudi Press Agency (SPA) reported, citing a Civil Defense spokesman.
The spokesman said that emergency teams responded after a "hostile projectile" launched by the Houthis fell in the area, according to the news agency.
He said the projectile hit a school in Najran, causing material damage.
Standard procedures for such incidents had been carried out, he added.
Earlier, the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government said it intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government against the Houthis since March 2015.
The group has controlled the capital Sanaa and several provinces since September 2014.

articles.title: Air Force and Space Force Shooting for Historic Recruiting Goals in 2027
articles.body:
The Air Force adjusted its fiscal 2026 recruiting goal down by a few hundred enlisted Airmen due to higher-than-expected retention and the number of available training slots—but it is aiming high in fiscal 2027 with its biggest goal for the Active-Duty Air Force in nearly 25 years, and the Space Force has set its largest recruitment target ever.
In an Oct. 1 release touting its successes in fiscal 2026, the Air Force Recruiting Service said it “met its recruiting goals” and enlisted 31,950 Airmen into the Air Force and 730 Guardians into the Space Force.
That Air Force number is 800 fewer than the 32,750 recruits the service cited in April when it announced it had accomplished its goal five months ahead of schedule. Headquarters Air Force shifted the goal this summer, a spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine, as it adjusted to the “realities” of retention and the number of slots available at Basic Military Training. Every military service has an end strength authorized every year by Congress, and if retention is higher than expected, the service can only add so many recruits. BMT also can be limited by resources or available training dates.
The Air Force spokesperson said recruits were not cut but rather added to the Delayed Entry Program where they await their turn to start Basic Military Training. There are currently 15,799 recruits in the DEP, giving the Air Force Recruiting Service a healthy backlog to draw upon to start the new fiscal year.
That could prove crucial as AFRS attempts to pull off a massive 2027. Another spokesperson confirmed its goals for next year are 36,300 non-prior service enlisted Airmen for the Active-Duty force, and 1,402 enlisted Guardians for the Space Force.
The Air Force’s recruiting goal hasn’t exceeded 35,000 since 2003, according to data compiled by Air & Space Forces Magazine. And the Space Force has never aimed for more than 900 new Guardians in its brief history.
Those big totals come as officials across the military say they are seeing historically high interest among potential recruits—and as the Pentagon pursues a major increase in resources and overall end strength.
“In [fiscal 2027], we will grow the force again by an additional 44,000 service members,” Pentagon comptroller Jules “Jay” W. Hurst III said in April. “This growth will provide the manpower needed to employ new capabilities, and it will improve readiness and quality of life by ensuring units are properly staffed for the missions we task them with.”
The Air Force in particular wants to increase its Active-Duty end strength by nearly 9,000, from 321,500 Airmen to 330,400, and the Space Force wants to add 2,800 Guardians, going from 10,400 to 13,200.
In its release, the Air Force Recruiting Service said it will adjust its strategies for 2027 “based on labor market trends, propensity-to-serve data, and career field demand signals.”
In a panel discussion last month at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Air Force Deputy Chief of Staff for manpower, personnel, and services Lt. Gen. Jefferson O’Donnell said much of the service’s growth would be more “restorative” than “additive,” reversing declines in manning for key career fields.
“We are focused on making sure that we are prioritizing those things like maintenance and logistics and security forces to fill in those spots where we have been taking significant risk across our service,” O’Donnell said.
